narration.full_text: Let's continue with the algebraic method, specifically the substitution technique. We'll pick up from where we left off, assuming we have already expressed one variable in terms of the other. So, if we have an equation like three y equals thirteen minus two x, our first step is to isolate y. We divide both sides by three, giving us y equals the quantity thirteen minus two x, all divided by three. This simplifies our expression for y. Now, with y expressed in terms of x, the next crucial step is to substitute this expression for y into the second equation of our system. Let's say our second equation is four x plus five y equals twenty-three. We replace y with the expression we just derived. So, it becomes four x plus five times the quantity thirteen minus two x, all divided by three, equals twenty-three. This substitution eliminates y, leaving us with an equation solely in terms of x. To simplify this equation and get rid of the fraction, we multiply both sides of the entire equation by three. This is a common technique to clear denominators. So, three times four x gives us twelve x. Three times five times the quantity thirteen minus two x, all divided by three, simply leaves us with five times thirteen minus two x, as the threes cancel out. And on the right side, three times twenty-three gives us sixty-nine. This results in the equation twelve x plus sixty-five minus ten x equals sixty-nine. We can now combine like terms to solve for x.
